newsitem.title: UK: EURO OIL TRADE AWAITS DETAILS ON IRAQI EXPORTS.
newsitem.headline: EURO OIL TRADE AWAITS DETAILS ON IRAQI EXPORTS.

text.p: Oil traders keen to sign contracts for the first Iraqi crude exports since May said on Wednesday they wanted more details from Baghdad before committing themselves.
Iraq's oil minister Muhammed Rasheed said exports should resume by the middle of August and that Baghdad would try to meet a permitted $2 billion target for oil sales by the December 6 deadline.

Pricing formulas submitted to the United Nations on Tuesday were competitive for European markets but an early flood of oil would undermine sour crude markets and make alternative grades more attractive, traders said.

"Dated Brent -$1.90 a barrel for Kirkuk Blend is attractive right now but if you see (Russian) Urals at -$1.00 then it will be a different matter," said a trader for a refiner which bought Iraqi crude during the first 180-day period of the oil-for-food deal.
Regional sour benchmark Russian Urals crude was already beginning to skid on Wednesday as three or four sellers offered second half August loading cargoes into a vacuum.
Offers were coming from around Dated Brent -65/-70 cents a barrel, basis cif Augusta, about 15 cents cheaper than the last reported deal.
"Most people are waiting because they are wary of buying something which may look cheap today but could be very expensive tomorrow," said a trader.

Companies negotiating with Iraq said they wanted to know whether the State Oil Marketing Organisation (SOMO) would be going "hell for leather" to meet the interim target of $1 billion by September 5, which would mean exporting at a rate of nearly two million bpd.
Rasheed said on Wednesday Iraq could export 1.8 million bpd but industry sources put the country's maximum sustainable capacity at 1.3-1.4 million bpd.
Even at the lower rate, spot markets would be thrown into turmoil, traders said.
"They want to collect as much cash as possible before the first 90-day period runs out in September," said one.

Some potential customers said they were seeking clarification about Baghdad's thinking on timing and contract length before asking for higher volumes than in the first period, when shipments averaged 700,000 bpd.
"One month ago we told them we would be happy to increase our volume but we have to talk to them about availability and how they intend to sort out the timing," said a trader.
Uncompetitive pricing formulas for the U.S. would also make Baghdad's job of placing extra barrels more difficult.
A lack of larger vessels has pushed up freight rates to well beyond where they stood at the end of the first period of sales, traders said.
"It's very tricky to talk about volumes at the moment because there's very little freight left," said a U.S. trader.
Some traders said SOMO may find a more sympathetic ear at the big European refineries who could be tempted by healthy margins to take oil into storage.
